definitions: A decrease in the wavelength of a photon or of light while in transit, corresponding to a higher frequency and a shift toward the blue end of the electromagnetic spectrum.
(said of light or a photon) To shift toward the blue end of the electromagnetic spectrum while in transit; to change to a shorter wavelength and a higher frequency.

blocks.text: In physics, a redshift is an increase in the wavelength, or equivalently, a decrease in the frequency, of electromagnetic radiation. The opposite change, a decrease in wavelength and increase in frequency and energy, is known as a blueshift.

images.alt: Doppler effect, yellow (c. 575 nm wavelength) ball appears greenish (blueshift to c. 565 nm wavelength) approaching observer, turns orange (redshift to c. 585 nm wavelength) as it passes, and returns to yellow when motion stops. To observe such a change in colour, the object would have to be travelling at approximately 5,200 km/s, or about 32 times faster than the speed record for the fastest space probe.

The lookback time by observed redshift up to z = 20 using parameters of the Planck mission in the standard model of cosmology.[45] There are websites for calculating distances from redshift.[30][31]

Comoving distance and lookback time for the Planck 2018 cosmology parameters, from redshift 0 to 15, with distance (blue solid line) on the left axis, and time (orange dashed line) on the right. Note that the time that has passed (in billions of years) from a given redshift until now is not the same as the distance (in giga light years) light would have travelled from that redshift, due to the expansion of the universe over the intervening period.
Matter waves (protons, electrons, photons, etc.) falling into a gravity well become more energetic and undergo observer-independent blueshifting.
